$comment: Canonical registry of government spending data sources. JSON (not YAML) so it is parseable by the Python ingest layer with zero dependencies AND directly loadable by the dashboard frontend. Every entry's `verified` field is false until scripts/check_sources.py probes it from a network that can actually reach these hosts.

sources.name: USAspending.gov API
sources.covers: Award-level federal spending: contracts, grants, loans, direct payments, plus agency budgetary resources by federal account and object class.
sources.update_cadence: daily (award data); monthly (account-level, after MTS close)
sources.history_from: FY2001, though award coverage is only reliable from FY2008 and account-level from FY2017
sources.notes: The backbone source. Mandated by the DATA Act. Critically: this reports OBLIGATIONS, not outlays — it will not reconcile to Treasury MTS and must never be summed alongside it. Historical rows are restated retroactively, so cached extracts drift from live queries.

sources.name: Treasury Fiscal Data — Monthly Treasury Statement
sources.covers: Actual receipts, outlays, and surplus/deficit by agency and by budget function. The authoritative 'money actually left the building' series.
sources.update_cadence: monthly, ~8th business day after month end
sources.notes: Pagination uses bracketed params (page[size], page[number]) which MUST be percent-encoded or curl/requests will mangle them. Filter syntax is ?filter=record_fiscal_year:eq:2025. This is the reconciliation anchor for every outlay figure in the dashboard.

sources.name: Treasury Fiscal Data — Daily Treasury Statement
sources.covers: Daily operating cash balance, deposits and withdrawals by category. Highest-frequency view of federal cash movement.
sources.update_cadence: each business day, ~4pm ET for prior day
sources.notes: Cash basis, not budget basis. Useful for a live 'pulse' tile but does not aggregate cleanly into fiscal-year budget totals.

sources.name: Treasury Fiscal Data — Debt & Interest
sources.covers: Debt to the Penny, average interest rates by security type, and monthly interest expense on the public debt.
sources.notes: Debt held by the public vs intragovernmental holdings vs total — the dashboard must label which one it shows. Total debt is the largest and least economically meaningful of the three.

sources.name: OMB Budget of the U.S. Government — Historical Tables
sources.covers: The long-run official series: outlays by agency (Table 4.1), by function (Table 3.1/3.2), by superfunction, receipts by source (Table 2.1), deficit (Table 1.1). Includes forward projections.
sources.update_cadence: annual, with the President's Budget release (typically February)
sources.notes: No API — bulk spreadsheet download only. whitehouse.gov URLs are reorganized by each incoming administration and old links rot; use the govinfo BUDGET collection as the stable archival mirror. This is the only source giving a consistent multi-decade series, so it anchors all long-run trend charts.

sources.name: Congressional Budget Office — Budget and Economic Data
sources.covers: Baseline budget projections, long-term outlook, historical budget data, and scoring of legislation.
sources.update_cadence: baseline twice yearly (Jan/Feb and update); long-term outlook annually
sources.notes: No API; stable-ish URLs per publication. The independent counterweight to OMB's numbers — showing both is the point, since the spread between CBO and OMB projections is itself a story.

sources.name: GovInfo API (GPO)
sources.covers: Archival, permanent copies of budget documents, appropriations bills, committee prints, and the U.S. Code.
sources.notes: Free key from api.data.gov (one key works across govinfo, congress.gov, and FAC). Use this as the durable mirror for OMB documents whose whitehouse.gov links rot.

sources.name: Congress.gov API
sources.covers: Appropriations and authorization bills, their text, status, sponsors, and committee action. Links legislation to the money it moves.
sources.notes: Free api.data.gov key. Provides the 'why' layer — connecting an appropriation act to the account-level spending that follows in USAspending.

sources.name: Federal Audit Clearinghouse API
sources.covers: Single Audit results for every entity expending $750k+ in federal awards: audit findings, questioned costs, material weaknesses, going-concern flags.
sources.history_from: FY2016 in the current API; earlier via bulk archive
sources.notes: PostgREST-style filtering (?auditee_state=eq.TX). The strongest 'audit' signal in the whole registry: it is the only source that systematically links a specific federal award to a finding of misuse. High priority given this repo's purpose.

sources.name: FPDS-NG Contract Feed
sources.covers: Raw, transaction-level federal contract actions — the upstream system USAspending's contract data is derived from.
sources.notes: More timely and more granular than USAspending, but ATOM XML with a quirky query DSL and a 10-record-per-page default. Use only when USAspending's latency or aggregation is genuinely insufficient.

sources.name: SAM.gov API
sources.covers: Entity registrations, Assistance Listings (formerly CFDA), contract opportunities, and the exclusions/debarment list.
sources.notes: Key request requires a SAM.gov account and some endpoints need a granted role — the slowest source to get access to, so schedule it early. Exclusions cross-referenced against active awards is a high-value audit check.

sources.name: PaymentAccuracy.gov — Improper Payments
sources.covers: Agency-reported improper payment rates and dollar estimates by program, plus root-cause categories and recovery amounts.
sources.notes: Self-reported by agencies and methodologically inconsistent between programs — an improper payment is not necessarily fraud, and the dashboard must say so. Still the headline number most users will come looking for.

sources.name: Oversight.gov — Inspector General Reports
sources.covers: Consolidated reports from all federal Inspectors General, including monetary findings and open recommendations.
sources.notes: Has an undocumented JSON endpoint behind the report search. Pairs with FAC to give the qualitative side of the audit story.

sources.name: CMS Data (Medicare & Medicaid)
sources.covers: Program spending, provider utilization and payment, Open Payments, and Medicaid/CHIP expenditure by state.
sources.update_cadence: varies by dataset, mostly quarterly or annual
sources.notes: Health programs are roughly a quarter of federal outlays, so a spending dashboard that treats HHS as a single bar is hiding the largest story in the budget.

sources.name: BEA API — National Accounts Government Tables
sources.covers: Government receipts and expenditures on a national-accounts basis (NIPA tables 3.1–3.10), including federal and state/local split.
sources.notes: Different accounting basis from the budget — reconciles to OMB only after documented adjustments. Also the source of the GDP price deflator needed for any inflation-adjusted chart.

sources.name: FRED API (St. Louis Fed)
sources.covers: Convenience layer over Treasury/BEA/CBO series: debt, deficit, outlays as share of GDP, deflators.
sources.license: Varies by series; FRED terms of use
sources.notes: Convenient but second-hand — always cite the primary source in the UI, not FRED, or the dashboard inherits FRED's revision lag. Useful series: GFDEBTN, FYFSD, FYONGDA188S.

sources.name: Census Annual Survey of State & Local Government Finances
sources.covers: The only nationally comparable dataset of state and local revenue and expenditure, by function and by unit of government.
sources.update_cadence: annual, with roughly a two-year lag
sources.notes: Two-year publication lag makes it useless for anything 'current', but it is the only way to compare states on a like-for-like basis. Census keys are free and instant.

sources.name: OPM FedScope
sources.covers: Federal civilian workforce headcount, salary, and grade by agency and location.
sources.notes: Bulk cube downloads only. Personnel cost is a large share of discretionary spending and is invisible in award-level data.

sources.name: Socrata Discovery API — State & Local Budget Datasets
sources.covers: Discovery across thousands of state, county, and municipal budget/checkbook datasets hosted on Socrata.
sources.notes: The practical entry point for state/local coverage: rather than hand-coding 50 state portals, search the catalog and normalize what comes back. Schemas are wildly inconsistent — expect per-publisher mapping work.

sources.name: Data.gov CKAN Catalog
sources.covers: Federated catalog of federal (and some state) datasets — used for discovering sources not yet in this registry.
sources.notes: Discovery tool, not a data source. Many listed links are dead; treat hits as leads to verify, not as sources to ingest.

caveats.summary: Obligations (USAspending) and outlays (Treasury MTS) are different measures and must never be summed or compared without conversion. A contract obligated in FY2024 may outlay across FY2025–2029. Every chart must label which measure it shows.

The federal fiscal year runs October 1 to September 30 and is named for the year it ends. Mixing FY and CY silently shifts a quarter of the data. State fiscal years differ again — most run July–June, but Texas, Alabama, Michigan, and New York do not.
Long-run spending charts in nominal dollars are misleading. Deflate using the BEA GDP price index, and offer share-of-GDP as the default view for multi-decade comparisons.
Recipient identifiers moved from DUNS to UEI in April 2022. Any recipient-level time series crossing that boundary needs a crosswalk or it will show spurious new entities and vanished incumbents.

Federal grants passed to states and re-granted to localities appear in federal, state, and local datasets. Naive consolidation across jurisdictions inflates totals substantially. Consolidated views must either pick one level or explicitly net out intergovernmental transfers.
USAspending and agency financial data are restated retroactively. A cached extract will diverge from a live query for the same period, so cache entries need an as-of timestamp surfaced in the UI.

USAspending account-level totals do not tie exactly to Treasury MTS because of coverage, timing, and basis differences. Some gap is expected and normal; the dashboard should display the residual rather than hide it, and alert only when it moves outside its historical band.

An improper payment is a payment that failed a documentation or eligibility test. Most are not fraud, and some are underpayments. Presenting the improper-payment total as a fraud figure would be a straightforward misrepresentation.
whitehouse.gov and agency budget URLs are reorganized between administrations. Prefer govinfo permalinks for anything archival.
